title: Mechanisms, subsystems, container
summary: How a real robot's code is organized.

say.never: A robot has a huge number of jobs: driving, shooting, lifting, reading sensors. If one giant file did all of them, finding one mistake would be like finding one sock in a messy house. So teams split the code into **three layers**, and each layer has exactly one job. When something breaks, you know which layer to look in.
say.bit: A robot has too many jobs for one file, so code is split into three layers with one job each: **mechanism**, **subsystem**, **container**. Bugs become easier to place.

board.code:
Container      // keeps the list of every subsystem on the robot
  Subsystem    // decides WHAT to do and WHEN
    Mechanism  // knows HOW to run one device
      motor, sensor

say.never: A **mechanism** looks after **one device**, like an elevator's motor and its height sensor. It knows *how* to do things, and it has no opinions about *when*. You give it orders ("go to 0.6 meters") and ask it questions ("how high are you?"). Think of it like a very good employee who only follows instructions. Mechanisms also follow the **read, think, write** loop: sensors are read before your code runs, and the motor order is sent after.
say.bit: A **mechanism** wraps one device (a motor and its sensor). It exposes orders and readings and makes no decisions. Sensors are read before your code runs and outputs are written after.

marks.label: a reading: what is true now

say.never: A **subsystem** is the manager. It owns one or more mechanisms and decides *what they should do right now*. Every 20 thousandths of a second its `updateLogic` method runs, looks at what the driver is doing, and gives its mechanisms their orders. Anything that asks the elevator to move goes through the subsystem, so there is only ever one boss.
say.bit: A **subsystem** owns mechanisms and decides what they do in `updateLogic`, which runs every loop. Everything else asks the subsystem instead of touching the mechanism.

marks.label: decide from what the driver is doing

say.never: The **robot container** is the front desk. It keeps the list of every subsystem on the robot, and **a subsystem that isn't on the list never runs**. That's a common beginner mistake: you write a whole subsystem, forget to add it to the list, and nothing happens. Every loop, the container tells each subsystem on its list to read its sensors, run its logic, and write its outputs.
say.bit: The **container** holds the list of subsystems. A subsystem that is not registered there never runs. Each loop it has every subsystem read, think and write.

marks.label: on the list, so it runs

say.never: Follow one press of a button down through the layers. A button is read by `OI`. The subsystem checks it and decides what that means. The subsystem gives an order to its mechanism. The mechanism turns the order into motor power. Meanwhile the sensor's reading travels back up the other way. Every layer only talks to its neighbour, which keeps things tidy.
say.bit: OI reads the button; the subsystem's logic turns it into mechanism orders; the mechanism drives the motor. Sensor readings flow back up the same way.

board.code:
button  ->  OI.getRaiseButton()
subsystem  ->  elevator.setTargetHeight(1.2)
mechanism  ->  motor power

sensor  ->  elevator.getHeight()  ->  subsystem checks it

say.never: Three good reasons. **Swap hardware:** if the team changes the elevator motor, only the mechanism changes, and the subsystem doesn't notice. **Reuse:** the same mechanism class can be used on two robots. **Teamwork:** one person can write the mechanism while another writes the subsystem, because they agree on the orders and readings between them. Your lesson's shooter is built exactly this way.
say.bit: Swap hardware without touching decisions, reuse mechanisms on other robots, and let teammates work on different layers in parallel.

steps.title: In your lesson: the three layers

say.never: A real robot's code is organized in three layers, and each has one job. At the bottom, a **mechanism** knows how to run one device (spin a wheel at a speed). In the middle, a **subsystem** decides *when* ("the button is held, so spin up"). At the top, the **container** keeps a list of all the subsystems.

board.code:
RobotContainer        // lists every subsystem
  ShooterSubsystem     // decides: when the button's held, spin up
    FlywheelMech       // knows how to spin a wheel at a speed
    RollerMech         // knows how to run a roller

say.bit: The drivetrain was a mechanism all along. This lesson wraps it in a subsystem and builds a shooter next to it.
